Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
</answer>

prompt: A 66-year-old man was admitted to this hospital because of malaise, weakness, and hypercalcemia. Thirty-five hours before admission, the patient was seen in an outpatient clinic affiliated with this hospital for evaluation of multiple problems, including a 3-week history of mild pain in the shoulder and left side of the neck, a 2-month history of muscle pain in the left leg that had occurred after a sports injury, listlessness, and a 3-month history of increasing frequency of urination, which occurred in small amounts up to twice each night and every 3 hours during the day and for which he had begun to restrict fluid. His neck pain had developed at work. Examination of the neck had revealed trapezius muscle spasm; naproxen, acetaminophen, and cyclobenzaprine had been administered, and the pain partially decreased. He also had a history of hypertension, benign prostatic hypertrophy, diverticulitis, lumbar disk disease, colonic polyps, ischial bursitis, chronic dyspepsia, nocturnal leg cramps, excessive alcohol use, and osteoarthritis of the shoulders, knees, and hips. Medications were amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, calcium carbonate for dyspepsia, tamsulosin, n–3 fatty acids, glucosamine, and a multivitamin, as well as ibuprofen and naproxen for musculoskeletal symptoms and, as needed, tadalafil and disulfiram. He had no known medication allergies. On examination, the patient appeared to be comfortable. The temperature was 36.7°C, the blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, the pulse 108 beats per minute, and the body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) 31.2. The posterior neck and occipital region on the left side were tender but had full range of motion, and the remainder of the examination was normal. The platelet count, red-cell indexes, and blood levels of glucose, thyrotropin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase were normal; other test results are shown inTable 1. Examination of the urine revealed turbid yellow fluid that was otherwise normal; urine culture was negative. That evening, after results of the blood tests were known, the patient was contacted and asked to return the next day for additional testing. Laboratory Data. Approximately 26 hours after the initial laboratory tests, the additional testing was performed. The blood levels of glucose, total protein, albumin, globulin, total bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase were normal; other test results are shown inTable 1. Eight hours later, when the test results were known, the patient was advised to go to the emergency department of this hospital for evaluation of potentially life-threatening abnormalities, and he was subsequently admitted. In the emergency department, the patient reported residual stiffness of the neck. He had had an influenza-like illness (with subjective fevers, diaphoresis, and nasal congestion) approximately 3 weeks before this evaluation that resolved spontaneously, and he reported chronic constipation that was unchanged. He had stopped drinking alcohol 4 years earlier and did not smoke tobacco or use illicit drugs. He lived with his wife, had adult children, and worked in an office. His father and a grandfather had died of lung cancer, a grandmother had died of a stroke, his mother had died of liver disease, and an uncle had had pancreatic cancer. On examination, the temperature was 36.8°C, the blood pressure 159/114 mm Hg, the pulse 109 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 97% while the patient was breathing ambient air. The remainder of the examination was normal. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with a ventricular rate of 101 beats per minute, a PR interval of 260 msec, a QRS complex of 136 msec, and a ratio of QT interval to QT interval corrected for heart rate of 318:412 msec; first-degree atrioventricular block and right bundle-branch block were present and had not been present 3 years earlier. A chest radiograph showed clear lungs and degenerative changes of the spine. The platelet count, prothrombin time, and prothrombin-time international normalized ratio were normal, as were blood levels of glucose, phosphorus, lactic acid, magnesium, total protein, albumin, globulin, total and direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, lipase, troponin T, andN-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide; other test results are shown inTable 1. Urinalysis revealed yellow, slightly cloudy urine, with a pH of 9.0, a specific gravity of 1.006, and 1+ occult blood by dipstick, as well as 0 to 2 red cells and 3 to 5 white cells per high-power field; squamous cells were present. The patient was admitted to the hospital, and additional imaging studies were obtained. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis, performed without the administration of intravenous or oral contrast material, revealed no evidence of cancer. CT of the chest revealed an indeterminate sclerotic lesion involving the right eighth rib (Figure 1). A radionuclide bone scan was recommended as a screening study for additional skeletal lesions. The bone scan revealed nonspecific abnormal uptake by the rib lesion and at the left ischium (Figure 2). Because there were concerns about cancer, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis was recommended for further evaluation and revealed a high-grade tear of the left common hamstring tendon at the ischial tuberosity attachment site. A fluoroscopically guided glucocorticoid injection had been performed at this location 11 months earlier. CT Scan of the Chest.A CT scan of the chest, obtained on hospital day 1, showed an indeterminate sclerotic lesion located at the anterolateral aspect of the right eighth rib (arrow). Radionuclide Bone Scan.A radionuclide bone scan, obtained on hospital day 2, showed abnormal uptake of the radiotracer by the rib lesion (not visible in this image). This nonspecific uptake could be explained by trauma or metastatic disease. On a posterior view of the pelvis, a second focus of abnormal uptake involved the left ischium (arrow). Additional tests were performed, and a diagnosis was made.

On examination, the patient appeared uncomfortable. The blood pressure was 140/76 mm Hg, the pulse 80 beats per minute, and the respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. The following day, on examination by her primary care physician, the temperature was 36.3°C and there was persistent right tonsillar exudate. Azithromycin was prescribed. Laboratory Data. Three days later, the patient was seen in the emergency department at Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary because of persistent odynophagia. She reported pain on the right side of her throat, which she rated at 10 on a scale of 0 to 10 (with 10 indicating the most severe pain), and headache. The pain did not radiate. She reported no fevers, chills, night sweats, malaise, or facial swelling. The mucous membranes were moist and pink, the salivary secretions were clear, and the floor of the mouth and the tongue were soft and nontender on palpation. Endoscopic examination revealed minimally edematous turbinates in the nasal cavity, shallow ulcerations along the posterior tonsillar wall, and erythema of the right arytenoid complex with overlying shallow ulcerations to the midline. Oxycodone–acetaminophen was administered. The patient returned home, with instructions to return for a follow-up visit in 1 week. Four days later, on repeat evaluation by her rheumatologist, she reported no relief in her throat pain and odynophagia, despite taking narcotic analgesic agents. The temperature was 36.6°C. The right tonsillar bed and right posterior pharynx were ulcerated and covered with gray exudate. The otolaryngologist was contacted and recommended administration of a short course of prednisone at a dose of 50 mg per day. Three days later, she returned to the emergency department at Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary for a scheduled follow-up visit. She reported persistent pain, which she rated at 10 out of 10, and associated decreasing oral intake. On endoscopic examination, there was decreased exudate on the right tonsil as compared with the amount of exudate seen on the previous examination, as well as resolving mucosal lesions on the posterior oropharyngeal wall and substantial improvement of the mucosal lesion on the right aryepiglottic fold. Prednisone was continued at a dose of 50 mg daily for 5 days and then decreased to a dose of 10 mg daily, and viscous lidocaine mouthwash was added. One week later (2 weeks after her initial presentation at Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary), the patient returned for follow-up in the emergency department, as advised. On examination, the temperature was 36.1°C and the other vital signs were normal. The right tonsil had persistent ulceration and was firm on palpation. Fiberoptic otolaryngoscopy revealed a tonsillar mass and ulcer extending along the right pharyngeal wall to the aryepiglottic fold, as well as persistent white exudate over the right aryepiglottic fold. The patient was widowed and lived alone, with her adult children living nearby. She was born in South America and had last visited 15 years earlier. Asymmetrically prominent lymph nodes were present in the right side of the neck (Figure 1E). A few lymph nodes were slightly irregular, with hazy margins. sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.

The timing fits.

The key here is the refeeding leading to electrolyte imbalances, specifically phosphate.

Myoglobinuria is more likely with rhabdo from low phosphate.
Also, the patient's history of anorexia and the refeeding protocol points to refeeding syndrome as the underlying cause.
So the most likely diagnosis is refeeding syndrome, which is causing the symptoms through hypophosphatemia leading to rhabdomyolysis and the associated dark urine.

Two months later, treatment with a combination of tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz was begun. At a follow-up appointment 1 month later, a gynecologic examination was performed to evaluate vaginal discharge, urinary frequency, and dysuria. Abnormalities were reported, and administration of a 10-day course of amoxicillin was begun. Four months after the initiation of ART, the CD4+ T-cell count had improved (Table 1). Laboratory Data. A peripheral blood smear reveals poikilocytes, schistocytes, and a decrease in the number of platelets. No fever or neurologic symptoms are present.

sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.
The patient is a 5-year-old with sudden bloody diarrhea, vomiting blood, hematuria, and renal failure after a flu-like illness.
The lab results show high BUN, which indicates kidney issues.
But fibrin degradation products and clotting times are normal, so maybe not DIC.
The blood smear shows poikilocytes, schistocytes, and low platelets.
Hmm, schistocytes are fragmented red blood cells, which usually point to something causing mechanical breakdown, like a microangiopathic process.
The symptoms started after a gastrointestinal illness.
The combination of GI bleeding, renal failure, and the blood findings makes me think of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
Typical HUS is caused by E. coli O157:H7, which can lead to bloody diarrhea followed by HUS.
The triad is microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (which the schistocytes suggest), thrombocytopenia (low platelets), and acute kidney injury.

The absence of neuro symptoms and normal clotting factors (since fibrinogen and clotting times are okay) fit HUS rather than TTP, which usually has more neurological issues and low platelets with a positive ADAMTS13 assay.
Also, in TTP, clotting factors might be abnormal, but here they are normal.
The presence of hematuria and renal failure aligns with HUS.
The initial flu-like illness could be the prodrome before the HUS sets in.
So putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome.

<answer>
Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
</answer>

prompt: A 40-year-old woman presents with bilateral conductive hearing loss, palpable purpura on the legs and hemoptysis. CT scan of the chest shows few thin-walled lung cavities bilaterally. Fuher investigations reveal total leukocyte count 12,000/mm3, red cell casts in the urine and, serum creatinine 2.3 mg/dL.

sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.
The patient is a 40-year-old woman with several symptoms.
First, she has bilateral conductive hearing loss.
Conductive hearing loss usually involves the outer or middle ear, so maybe something like otitis or a tumor?
But then there's palpable purpura on her legs.
Purpura could be from vasculitis or coagulation issues.
Hemoptysis suggests something in the lungs, maybe an infection or a vascular problem.
The CT chest shows thin-walled lung cavities.

Thin-walled cavities make me think of certain infections like tuberculosis or maybe a fungal infection, but also conditions like Wegener's granulomatosis (now called granulomatosis with polyangiitis).
Wait, the presence of red cell casts in the urine and elevated creatinine points to kidney involvement.
Red cell casts are a sign of glomerular damage, so maybe a vasculitis affecting the kidneys.
The leukocytosis (12,000) could be due to infection or inflammation.
Let me think about the combination of symptoms: hearing loss (middle ear involvement?), purpura (skin vasculitis), lung cavities, renal impairment with casts.
That classic triad of upper respiratory (like ear issues), lung, and kidney problems is a hallmark of GPA (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis).
Wait, GPA typically affects the upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys.
The conductive hearing loss might be due to middle ear involvement.
The purpura could be from cutaneous vasculitis.
The lung cavities are consistent with necrotizing lesions.
The labs: leukocytosis, renal dysfunction with red cell casts all fit.
Another possibility could be microscopic polyangiitis, but that usually doesn't involve the upper respiratory as much.
Also, the presence of red cell casts in urine and the renal function being affected (creatinine 2.3) points more towards GPA.
Let me check if the criteria for GPA are met.
The American College of Rheumatology criteria include sinusitis, oral ulcers, respiratory tract involvement, etc.
But the key here is the combination of ear, lung, and kidney issues.
So putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (formerly Wegener's).
I don't think it's Churg-Strauss because there's no mention of asthma or eosinophilia.
The thin-walled cavities might also be seen in other conditions, but with the renal and ear involvement, GPA is the top choice.

prompt: A baby born to a young woman whose pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios was placed in the intensive care unit because of repeated vomiting containing bile. The stomach was markedly distended, and only small amounts of meconium had passed through the anus.

sentences.s: Okay, let's see.
The case is about a newborn with some specific issues.
The mom had polyhydramnios during pregnancy.
The baby is in the ICU because of repeated vomiting that contains bile.
Also, the stomach is really distended, and only a little meconium has passed through the anus.
Hmm, first, polyhydramnios in pregnancy can be a sign of something affecting the baby's GI tract.
Maybe the baby can't swallow amniotic fluid properly, leading to more amniotic fluid buildup.
But the main issue here is the vomiting with bile and the distended stomach.
Vomiting that has bile is important because bile comes from the duodenum.
So if bile is present, that means the obstruction is probably beyond the stomach, maybe in the small intestine.
The fact that meconium is only a little and passed through the anus suggests that there's a blockage somewhere.
Normally, meconium should pass shortly after birth.
The key symptoms here are vomiting (bilious), abdominal distension, and delayed meconium.
That makes me think of intestinal obstruction.
The most common causes in a newborn could be things like Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, or maybe an anatomical defect like intestinal atresia.
Hirschsprung's disease is when there's a lack of nerve cells in the intestine, leading to obstruction.
But usually, Hirschsprung's might present with failure to pass meconium within the first 24-48 hours.
The meconium here is mentioned as only small amounts, so maybe not the classic presentation.
Meconium ileus is often associated with cystic fibrosis.
It's a blockage in the ileum due to thick meconium.
That would cause similar symptoms, but I think meconium ileus usually presents with the baby not passing meconium at all, and maybe a distended abdomen.
But the presence of some meconium might be a clue against it, or maybe it's just a small amount because of the blockage.
Another possibility is duodenal atresia.
The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine.
If there's a blockage there, the baby would vomit bile because the obstruction is beyond the stomach.
Also, polyhydramnios is more commonly associated with duodenal atresia because the baby can't swallow the amniotic fluid properly, leading to increased amniotic fluid.
Wait, duodenal atresia typically presents with bilious vomiting, a distended abdomen, and failure to pass meconium.
The mom's polyhydramnios fits with that.
So maybe that's the diagnosis here.
Alternatively, annular pancreas or malrotation with volvulus could be possibilities, but those might present a bit differently.
Malrotation can lead to midgut volvulus, which is an emergency, but the timing here is at birth.
So putting it all together: polyhydramnios in the mother, bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and minimal meconium.
The most likely is duodenal atresia.
Let me confirm the classic triad.
Duodenal atresia is characterized by the triad of polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting, and a double-bubble sign on abdominal X-ray (which shows the two parts of the duodenum).
Since the case mentions the stomach is markedly distended, that might correspond to the double bubble (stomach and dilated duodenum segment).
Therefore, the diagnosis should be duodenal atresia.

<answer>

prompt: A 31-year-old woman has experienced increasing malaise for the past 4 months. Physical examination yields no remarkable findings. sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.

The physical exam is unremarkable, so no obvious signs like jaundice or hepatomegaly.
Let's look at the lab results.

The total protein is 6.4, which is a bit low, but albumin is 3.6, which is within the normal range (usually 3.5-5.0).

The transaminases (AST and ALT) are both elevated—AST 67 and ALT 91.
Those are a bit high, but not super high.

So the pattern here is mainly elevated ALT and AST with a slight bilirubin increase.

Let me recall: autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) typically has positive ANA and SMA.
LKM-1 is more associated with type 2 AIH, which is usually in children but can occur in adults.
Type 1 AIH is more common in adults and has ANA and SMA.
But here, both ANA and LKM-1 are positive.
Hmm, maybe that's a bit conflicting?
Or maybe in some cases, both can be present?
The liver biopsy shows minimal portal mononuclear infiltrates, minimal interface hepatitis, and mild portal fibrosis.
In AIH, you usually see more pronounced inflammation, like lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis), and more fibrosis.
But the biopsy here is described as minimal.
Wait, but maybe it's early disease?
Or maybe another condition?
Wait, the total protein is low (6.4), but albumin is normal.
That might suggest that the liver is okay in terms of synthetic function, but maybe there's another cause of hypoalbuminemia, like malnutrition or loss.
But the main issue here is the liver enzymes.
The positive autoantibodies are key here.
ANA and SMA are classic for AIH type 1.
LKM-1 is more for type 2, but type 2 is more common in children.
However, the presence of both might be a clue.
Alternatively, maybe the LKM-1 is a red herring?
Or perhaps the biopsy findings are not as severe as expected in AIH.
But the autoantibodies are strongly positive, which is a big point for AIH.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) usually has anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) positive, which isn't mentioned here.
PSC would have different antibodies, maybe.
But the bilirubin isn't that high, and ALP is normal, so maybe not.
Another thought: the minimal biopsy findings might suggest early AIH or a less active phase.
The criteria for AIH include autoantibodies, elevated liver enzymes, interface hepatitis on biopsy, and exclusion of other causes.
The biopsy here has minimal inflammation but still some interface changes and fibrosis.
Maybe it's a mild form or early stage.
Alternatively, could it be drug-induced liver injury?
But the patient's history isn't mentioned here.
The labs don't show a pattern pointing to that.
Also, the autoantibodies are positive, which is more indicative of autoimmune.
Another possibility is overlap syndromes, but that usually combines features of AIH and PBC or PSC, which isn't indicated here.
Putting it all together: the positive ANA and SMA, along with LKM-1 (though that's more type 2), but the clinical scenario fits autoimmune hepatitis.
The biopsy, even if minimal, still shows some features consistent with autoimmune process.
The absence of viral causes and the autoantibodies make AIH the most likely diagnosis.
The slight elevation in bilirubin and transaminases, even if not extremely high, can be part of the picture.
Maybe the patient is in an early stage or has a milder form.
The key is the combination of autoantibodies and the histology, even if not severe.

prompt: A 22-year-old woman from a large Italian family is screened for a familial blood disorder. The results of laboratory studies include a hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL and a smear displaying mild microcytosis, hypochromia, and a few target cells. sentences.s: Okay, let's see.
The patient is a 22-year-old woman from a large Italian family being screened for a familial blood disorder.
The lab results show a hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL, which is below the normal range (usually around 12-16 g/dL for women), indicating anemia.
The blood smear shows mild microcytosis and hypochromia, which are typical of iron deficiency anemia or thalassemia.
But there are also a few target cells, which can be seen in thalassemia or maybe some other conditions like liver disease, but given the context of a familial disorder, thalassemia is more likely.
The hemoglobin electrophoresis shows an increased Hb A2 level of 7.5%.
Normal Hb A2 is usually around 2-3.5%, so this is elevated.
I remember that in beta-thalassemia trait, Hb A2 is elevated, typically between 3.5-7.5%, so this patient's Hb A2 is at the higher end of that range.
In alpha-thalassemia, the Hb A2 is usually normal or slightly decreased, so that's probably not it.
The presence of target cells is more suggestive of beta-thalassemia.
Also, the patient is from an Italian family, and beta-thalassemia is more common in Mediterranean populations, which aligns with her background.
Iron deficiency can also cause microcytic anemia with hypochromia, but target cells are less common in iron deficiency.
Plus, in iron deficiency, Hb A2 is typically normal.
Since the Hb A2 is elevated here, that points more towards thalassemia.
So putting it all together: microcytic, hypochromic anemia with target cells, elevated Hb A2, and a familial component in someone of Mediterranean descent.
The most likely diagnosis is beta-thalassemia trait.

prompt: A 45 year old father presents with sleep deprivation, lethargy headache, and low mood two months after knowing that his son is suffering from leukemia. He interacts reasonably well with others, but has absented himself from work.

sentences.s: Okay, let's see.

Wait, so the timing is two months after the stressor.
That's within the timeframe for adjustment disorder, which typically develops within three months of a stressor and lasts up to six months.

The headaches and lethargy could be physical symptoms related to stress or the depression itself.

Anxiety disorders?

Post-traumatic stress disorder?

The patient had been in her usual state of health until 1 year before this admission, when fatigue and weight loss developed and she had abnormal results on liver-function tests after undergoing cholecystectomy for presumed acalculous cholecystitis. A chest radiograph obtained 1 month before admission (Panels B and C) shows bilateral, perihilar, diffuse ground-glass opacities with additional patchy opacities at the lung bases and no evidence of pleural effusion. Seven months before this admission, a submandibular mass and swelling developed; 1 month later, examination of a biopsy specimen of the mass revealed granulomatous sialadenitis. A liver biopsy was performed to investigate the patient’s abdominal distention, poor appetite, and persistently abnormal liver-function test results, which were suggestive of cholestasis. The liver-biopsy specimen showed evidence of granulomatous hepatitis; portal and periportal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation that was associated with multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes, and some plasma cells; and stage 1 to 2 (portal and periportal) fibrosis. A diagnosis of sarcoidosis was made on the basis of the biopsy results of the submandibular gland and liver and the presence of hypercalcemia and an elevated angiotensin-converting–enzyme level. In the emergency department, the patient reported progressive dyspnea on exertion and being unable to climb stairs in her home. There was no chest pain, edema in the legs, weight gain, or orthopnea. In addition to methotrexate and prednisone, her medications included omeprazole and trazodone. Her father had hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and one son had ulcerative colitis. Both maternal grandparents had had tuberculosis, but the patient had not had contact with them; her mother had latent tuberculosis. The patient had no known drug allergies. prompt: A previously healthy 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because of recurrent abdominal cramps, bloating, and diarrhea for 4 months. She describes her stools as greasy, foul-smelling, and difficult to flush. During this time she has had a 6-kg (13.2-lb) weight loss. She has no personal or family history of serious illness. Physical examination shows pallor and cheilitis. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 11 g/dL. Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine are within the reference range. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative and stool microscopy reveals no pathogens and no leukocytes. Analysis of a 24-hour stool sample shows 12 g of fat. The patient is asked to consume 25 g of d-xylose. Five hours later, its concentration is measured in urine at 2 g (N = > 4 g/5 h). The test is repeated after a two-week course of rifaximin, but the urinary concentration of d-xylose remains the same. What is the most likely diagnosis?

sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.
The patient is a 20-year-old woman with a 4-month history of abdominal cramps, bloating, and diarrhea.
The stools are greasy and foul-smelling, which makes me think of malabsorption.

The lab results confirm anemia with a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL.
The stool tests are negative for occult blood, pathogens, and leukocytes, so it's not an infection or inflammatory bowel disease.
The key here is the 24-hour stool analysis showing 12g of fat.
Normal fat excretion is less than 7g/day, so this is definitely steatorrhea, pointing to malabsorption.
The d-xylose test is next.
The patient's urine only had 2g after 5 hours, but normal is over 4g. D-xylose is a sugar that's absorbed in the small intestine, so low levels in urine suggest a problem with absorption.
But since the test was repeated after rifaximin (an antibiotic) and didn't improve, that suggests it's not due to bacterial overgrowth.
Because bacterial overgrowth can impair d-xylose absorption, but treating it with rifaximin didn't help here, so the issue is likely structural or another cause.
Possible causes of malabsorption include celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, Crohn's disease, Whipple's disease, or maybe an anatomical issue like short bowel syndrome.
But since the stool doesn't show blood or leukocytes, inflammatory conditions like Crohn's might be less likely.
Celiac is possible, but she's young and the d-xylose test might help differentiate.
In celiac, the damage to the villi would impair d-xylose absorption, but so would other malabsorption issues.
However, since the rifaximin didn't help, bacterial overgrowth is less likely.
Another thought: pancreatic insufficiency.
If the pancreas isn't producing enough enzymes, fat isn't digested, leading to steatorrhea.

prompt: A 20-year-old woman was seen in the neurology clinic of this hospital because of seizures and progressive dystonia. The patient had been well until she was 3 years of age, when she began to have recurrent falls, difficulty walking, and seizures. A diagnostic evaluation at another hospital included a muscle biopsy, electroencephalography, and electroretinography, as well as analysis of the carnitine profile, visual-evoked potentials, and the enzymatic activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain; the test results were reportedly interpreted as inconclusive. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was performed; T2-weighted images reportedly showed areas of abnormal hyperintensity in the basal ganglia bilaterally. Therapy with carbamazepine and a multivitamin was initiated. During the next 15 years, progressive stepwise deterioration, including worsening dystonia and dysarthria, occurred; cognitive function was not affected. Exacerbations of her neurologic decline were precipitated by acute intercurrent illnesses and recurrent seizures from which she did not have complete recovery. Five years before the current presentation, anticonvulsant medications were stopped for 1 month. During that period, three flurries of generalized tonic–clonic seizures occurred. During admission to a second hospital, the complete blood count, oxygen saturation, blood levels of calcium and magnesium, and results of liver- and renal-function tests were normal. Medications on discharge included carbamazepine,l-carnitine, coenzyme Q10, and vitamin B complex. On follow-up at that hospital 2 months later, the patient reportedly had dysarthria, dystonic posturing of both arms (especially the hands), and an ataxic gait. Strength was 3+/5 in the distal arms and 5/5 in the proximal arms. Approximately 2.8 years before the current presentation, the patient was evaluated at a third hospital. MRI of the head was performed; T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images again showed areas of abnormal hyperintensity in the basal ganglia bilaterally, with mild associated volume loss. The MRI was significantly degraded by susceptibility artifacts that were produced by orthodontic braces. The blood lactate level was 1.6 mmol per liter (14.4 mg per deciliter; reference range at this hospital, 0.5 to 2.2 mmol per liter [4.5 to 19.8 mg per deciliter]), and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lactate level was 1.2 mmol per liter (10.8 mg per deciliter; reference range at this hospital, 0.6 to 2.2 mmol per liter [5.4 to 19.8 mg per deciliter]). A preliminary diagnosis of mitochondrial cytopathy was made. Between 17 and 11 months before the current presentation, examinations were performed at the second hospital while the patient was receiving levetiracetam and trihexyphenidyl. Speech difficulties, limb rigidity, and spasticity of the left upper leg were noted. She was referred to the epilepsy clinic of this hospital. On presentation to this hospital, the patient reported dysarthric speech and painful dystonia of her hands and limbs (particularly her legs). The dystonia was associated with gait deterioration that had led to use of a wheelchair. Cognitive function was not affected. Her most recent seizure had occurred 1 year before this assessment. The patient was the fourth child of healthy consanguineous parents (first cousins). She had been born after a full-term gestation, with no complications. Her birth weight was 3750 g. Medications were levetiracetam, pyridoxine, thiamine, and trihexyphenidyl. She had no known allergies. She lived with her family in the Arabian Peninsula; she spoke Arabic and some English, attended a regular high school, and did not drink alcohol, smoke tobacco, or use illicit drugs. She had three older brothers who were healthy. She had a 6-year-old sister with a similar illness that had started when she was 3 years of age, when she had an episode of bloody diarrhea and then began to have dystonia of the right foot, difficulty walking, and seizures. On evaluation at that time, the sister had a peak blood lactate level of 11.7 mmol per liter (105.4 mg per deciliter) and a peak CSF lactate level of 2.3 mmol per liter (20.7 mg per deciliter). Genetic testing for the MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes) and the Leigh syndrome was reportedly negative, and levels of urinary organic acids were normal. The sister underwent MRI of the head during the acute phase of her disease. T2-weighted images showed nonenhancing areas of abnormal, diffuse hyperintensity in the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, thalami, midbrain, and cerebellum. Repeat imaging studies obtained 10 months later showed resolution of most of the signal abnormalities, although residual signal abnormalities and volume loss were present in the basal ganglia. On examination at this hospital, which was performed with the assistance of an interpreter, the patient was alert and her mental status was normal. She had severe dysarthria, but her speech was fluent, with no paraphasic errors. Cranial-nerve function was intact, and visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes. She had fluctuating dystonia of the hands, arms, legs, and feet that was more prominent on the left side than on the right side. Strength was normal throughout. The plantar reflex was extensor in the left foot and was mute in the right foot; deep-tendon reflexes were normal. The gait was slow, wide-based, and dystonic, with inversion and internal rotation of both feet. The remainder of the examination was normal. MRI of the head was performed without the administration of intravenous contrast material. prompt: A 45-year-old man was admitted to this hospital because of a new rash. The patient had been well until 2 p.m. on the day before admission, when nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting developed. The next morning, he was seen at another hospital, where he reported increasing asthma and right-sided back pain, which he rated at 10 on a scale of 0 to 10 (with 10 indicating the most severe pain). On examination, he was in moderate distress. The temperature was 36.5°C, the blood pressure 112/69 mm Hg, the pulse 125 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 94% while he was breathing ambient air. The mucous membranes were dry, and he had scattered inspiratory wheezes, pallor and decreased skin turgor, and puncture wounds on his arms and hands. Laboratory-test results are shown inTable 1. Urinalysis was normal. Ipratropium and albuterol were given by inhalation, and famotidine, ondansetron, normal saline, metoclopramide, and methylprednisolone were administered intravenously; hydromorphone was then administered because of increasing pain. Laboratory Data. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis, performed at the other hospital after the oral (but not intravenous) administration of contrast material, did not reveal any findings of acute disease (e.g., bowel distention or bowel-wall thickening) to explain the patient's severe pain and vomiting. The spleen appeared small, measuring 8 cm in the maximal craniocaudal dimension (normal range for adults, 12 to 14 cm), with at least two granulomas. There was also mild enlargement of the caudate lobe of the liver. Shortly after CT was performed, skin mottling and livedo developed, and additional history was obtained. Three days before presentation, the patient was bitten on his hands and forearms while bathing his dog; later that day, his wife washed the wounds with hydrogen peroxide. Levofloxacin, piperacillin, and tazobactam were administered at the other hospital. He was transferred to this hospital, arriving approximately 23 hours after the onset of symptoms. On presentation, the patient reported malaise, shaking chills, a burning pins-and-needles sensation in his limbs, and diffuse body pain that he rated at 10 out of 10. He had had head trauma caused by a rusty nail a few days before presentation and dental extractions 1 to 2 weeks before presentation. He also had a history of asthma, mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse (with recent consumption of up to 18 beers daily); he had stopped drinking 3 days before admission. His medications were citalopram and omeprazole daily, alprazolam as needed for anxiety, and albuterol and a combination of budesonide and formoterol, which were administered by inhalation as needed for asthma. He was allergic to codeine, and tramadol had caused auditory hallucinations. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily (and had done so for 30 years), and he had used illicit drugs in the past. He reported no recent tick bites or exposures to other animals, sick persons, raw oysters, freshwater, or saltwater. He lived with his wife and his dog, which was fully vaccinated. He worked sporadically and had recently installed air-conditioning systems. His parents both died at 72 years of age from myocardial infarctions. On examination, the patient appeared ill, anxious, and diaphoretic. The temperature was 35.6°C, the blood pressure 154/102 mm Hg, the pulse 110 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 100% while he was breathing ambient air. The abdomen was soft and nondistended, with normal bowel sounds and mild tenderness in the lower quadrants and without guarding or rebound. Diffuse, purple, blanching livedo extended over his arms and legs, there was some mottling on his flanks and abdomen, and his fingers and ears were slightly blue (Figure 1). There were numerous lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks on his hands and forearms; the largest mark on his right forearm (3 to 4 cm in length) had a surrounding border (5 to 7 cm in diameter) with a purplish tinge and without exudate, crepitus, or bullae. Capillary refill occurred in 5 seconds. The remainder of the examination was normal, as were blood levels of glucose, direct and total bilirubin, phosphorus, globulin, lipase, alkaline phosphatase, methemoglobin, and haptoglobin; other test results are shown inTable 1. A chest radiograph with poor inspiratory effort showed elevation of the left hemidiaphragm that did not have an obvious cause; there was no evidence of pneumonia. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm at a rate of 132 beats per minute and low-voltage QRS complexes, with Q waves and ST-segment elevations (≤2 mm) in the anterior leads. Vancomycin, cefepime, metronidazole, alprazolam, and 3 liters of normal saline were administered, and calcium and magnesium were given as needed. During the next year, hot flashes developed, and a diagnosis of primary ovarian failure was made when the patient was 32 years of age. When the patient was 33.5 years of age, ultrasonography of the thyroid reportedly revealed a small amount of thyroid tissue on the right side and a new echogenic thyroid nodule on the left side, which displaced the carotid artery. Cytologic examination of fine-needle aspirate from the nodule was reportedly suspicious for a follicular neoplasm. She was referred to the endocrinology clinic at this hospital. The patient reported no hoarseness, dysphagia, shortness of breath, or neck pain. She had a history of fibrocystic breast disease and had undergone multiple, benign breast biopsies, and she had been exposed to diethylstilbestrol in utero. She had undergone a right ovarian cystectomy, stripping of varicose veins, and tonsillectomy, as well as excision of skin lesions on the face, with unknown histopathological findings. There was no history of neck irradiation. Medications included levothyroxine, calcitriol, estradiol (administered by a transdermal patch), and oral progesterone (12 days per month). She had an allergy to shellfish (manifested by angioedema) and had no known allergies to medications. She was married, had no children, and worked in an office. She drank alcohol in moderation and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. Her mother had thyroiditis, her father had had colonic polyps, and a sister had had a small goiter at 31 years of age. On examination, the blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, the pulse 78 beats per minute, and the weight 95.3 kg. The patient was obese, with facial acne. There was a healed surgical scar on the neck and a mobile, rubbery nodule, 4 cm in diameter, in the upper left thyroid bed. A positive Chvostek's sign (brisk twitching of the lips) was elicited on percussion of the homolateral masseter region, and the remainder of the examination was normal. Eight months later, the left thyroid nodule measured 6 cm in diameter on examination; computed tomography (CT) of the neck, performed without the administration of contrast material, and ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous mass, 48 mm in diameter, with central calcification at the level of the left thyroid bed. Completion thyroidectomy of the left lobe with partial strap-muscle resection was performed. Pathological examination showed an adenomatous goiter and no evidence of cancer. Postoperatively, liothyronine (l-isomer of triiodothyronine [T3]) was administered. The blood level of thyrotropin was 26.4 μU per milliliter (normal range, 0.4 to 5.0) and the level of thyroglobulin 1.8 ng per milliliter (normal range, 4 to 40). The thyroglobulin antibody and urinary iodine levels were normal. The 24-hour uptake of radioactive iodine (iodine-123) was 9%, and the scan of the thyroid with iodine-123 showed a single focus of intense uptake in the left thyroid bed and a subtle focus of uptake in the right thyroid bed. Whole-body scanning performed 3 days after an oral dose of 49.9 mCi of iodine-131 and immediately after the intravenous injection of 39.6 MBq of technetium-99m pertechnetate, with multiple dual-photon images of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, showed iodine uptake in the midline and the right side of the neck, findings suggestive of a remnant of thyroid tissue. When the patient was 35.5 years old, analogue mammography performed at another hospital revealed abnormalities in the left breast. The ductal carcinoma in situ cells expressed both estrogen-receptor and progesterone-receptor proteins. Treatment with estrogen and progesterone was stopped, and a course of radiation therapy was administered to the left breast. At the age of 36.5 years, the patient returned to the endocrinology clinic at this hospital for follow-up. On examination, there were micronodular lesions on the gingiva and tongue (Figure 1A and 1B); the remainder of the examination was unchanged. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed a small hypoechoic region of the left thyroid bed that measured 6 mm in maximal dimension, an increase from 3 mm 1.5 years earlier. The blood level of thyroglobulin was less than 0.2 ng per milliliter. Blood levels of calcium, thyrotropin, and thyroglobulin antibody were normal. prompt: An 87-year-old man with multiple chronic medical problems was seen in an outpatient clinic of this hospital because of sore throat and fatigue. The patient had been in his usual health until several weeks before presentation, when hoarseness, sore throat, and increasing fatigue developed. At the urging of his family, he was seen by his physician in an outpatient clinic of this hospital. He reported hoarseness, increasing facial puffiness, and periorbital swelling, with no chest pain, dyspnea, or new joint pains or muscle aches. The patient had hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease. Two months earlier, the creatinine level was 2.22 mg per deciliter (196 μmol per liter; reference range, 0.60 to 1.50 mg per deciliter [53 to 133 μmol per liter]), which was stable, as compared with values obtained the previous year. He also had hypothyroidism, with a normal thyrotropin level 8 months earlier (3.38 μU per milliliter [reference range, 0.40 to 5.00]), as well as gastroesophageal reflux disease, esophageal motility disorder, an abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic back pain, depression related to the death of his wife several years before, and recurrent urinary tract infections. In the past, he had had pneumonia and had undergone angioplasty of the right renal artery (10 years earlier), a cholecystectomy, a lobectomy of the right middle lobe due to a spiculated nodule that was found to be benign, photoselective vaporization of the prostate due to obstructive benign prostatic hypertrophy (2 months before this presentation), and wrist surgery. Medications included atenolol, vitamin D3, a fluticasone propionate and salmeterol inhaler, aspirin, citalopram, a fluticasone nasal spray, atorvastatin, omeprazole, and levothyroxine. Lisinopril had caused a cough, and zolpidem tartrate had caused nightmares. The patient was retired and lived alone. He could independently perform activities of daily living, and he managed his own medications. His three children lived nearby and were in frequent contact with him, but he came to most medical appointments unaccompanied. He was under the regular care of an internist, a nephrologist, a cardiologist, and a urologist. Immunizations were up to date. He had stopped smoking many years earlier and did not drink alcohol. His father had died of liver cancer, and a son had sarcoidosis; his two other children were healthy. On examination, the patient was pleasant, smiling, and in no distress; he spoke with a hoarse voice. The blood pressure was 130/72 mm Hg, the pulse 59 beats per minute, the oxygen saturation 96% while he was breathing ambient air, the weight 86.8 kg (approximately 4.5 kg greater than it had been 1 month earlier), and the body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) 29.9. There was facial swelling and periorbital edema; the remainder of the examination was normal. Blood levels of glucose, total protein, albumin, globulin, calcium, phosphorus, and total bilirubin and the plasma anion gap were normal; other test results are shown inTable 1. An appointment with an otolaryngologist was scheduled, and the patient returned home. Two days later, when the results of the laboratory tests were known, he was instructed by his physician to stop taking atorvastatin, and a follow-up appointment was scheduled for 9 days later in the outpatient clinic for repeat blood tests. Laboratory Data. Seven days after presentation, the patient called his doctor’s office at his daughter’s urging to report persistent hoarseness and swelling of his face and abdomen, which he indicated had been present for months but had, according to his daughter, worsened recently. Four days later, 11 days after presentation, he was seen in the outpatient clinic, where he reported markedly worsening fatigue, especially after walking, with associated dyspnea, facial edema, weight gain, cough that produced white mucus, and laryngitis. He reported no chest pain or worsening arthralgias and stated that he was taking all his medications. Chest radiographs were obtained. Frontal and lateral chest radiographs (Figure 1) showed no changes, as compared with chest radiographs and computed tomographic scans obtained 9 months previously. In addition to sutures from the lobectomy of the right middle lobe, there were small reticulonodular opacities at the right base, findings suggestive of scarring due to recurrent aspiration or prior infection. No evidence of pulmonary edema, lymphadenopathy, or a mediastinal mass was seen. Chest Radiographs.Frontal and lateral chest radiographs (Panels A and B, respectively) were obtained 11 days after presentation. The box in each panel shows the area that is enlarged in the inset. There are reticulonodular opacities at the base of the right lung (Panel A, inset) and chain sutures from a lobectomy of the right middle lobe (Panel B, inset). Incidentally noted are a healed right-rib fracture (Panel A, arrowhead) and interposition of the transverse colon between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm (Panels A and B, arrows). A complete blood count and a white-cell differential count were normal, as were blood levels of glucose, calcium, total protein, albumin, globulin, total bilirubin, and C-reactive protein; other test results are shown inTable 1. A diagnostic test result was received.

A friend who had eaten the same meal as the patient the evening before admission had vomited once shortly thereafter but had not become progressively ill. prompt: A 53-year-old man was admitted to this hospital because of shock and recurrent ventricular tachycardia after defibrillator placement for nonischemic cardiomyopathy. The patient had been in his usual state of health until 4 weeks before this admission, when he was on vacation in the Caribbean and his wife noted that he was unresponsive, “gurgling,” and diaphoretic in the early morning. When he awoke, he reported chest pain, palpitations, and light-headedness. The patient was taken by ambulance to a local hospital, where the heart rate was 65 beats per minute, the blood pressure 100/56 mm Hg, and the oxygen saturation 100% while he was breathing oxygen through a nasal cannula at a rate of 2 liters per minute. The troponin T level was 1.56 ng per milliliter (normal range, <0.01), and the lactate level was 1.9 mmol per liter (17 mg per deciliter; normal range, 0.5 to 1.6 mmol per liter [5 to 14 mg per deciliter]). A complete blood count and levels of electrolytes, magnesium, calcium, and amylase were normal, as were results of tests of renal and thyroid function; ad-dimer level was undetectable. While the patient was in the local hospital, monomorphic ventricular tachycardia developed at a heart rate of 201 beats per minute; electrocardioversion resulted in restoration of sinus rhythm. Aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin, rosuvastatin, amiodarone, and tirofiban were administered. The patient was transferred by air to a hospital in Florida. On examination at the second hospital, the temperature was 36.8°C, the heart rate 57 beats per minute, the blood pressure 122/90 mm Hg, the respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 99% while the patient was breathing oxygen through a nasal cannula at a rate of 2 liters per minute. The remainder of the examination was normal. The blood troponin I level was 116.00 ng per milliliter (normal range, ≤0.05). A complete blood count, results of renal-function tests, levels of electrolytes and thyrotropin, and the prothrombin and partial-thromboplastin times were normal. An electrocardiogram (Figure 1A) showed sinus bradycardia, a ventricular ectopic beat, first-degree atrioventricular delay, and delayed intraventricular conduction. Aspirin, amiodarone, enoxaparin, and atorvastatin were administered. Ventricular tachycardia recurred at a heart rate of 176 beats per minute. Despite the administration of an intravenous bolus of amiodarone, ventricular tachycardia persisted. Electrocardioversion restored sinus rhythm. The patient was admitted to the hospital, and cardiac studies were performed. Initial Cardiac Studies, Obtained at the Second Hospital.Cardiac studies were obtained during the patient’s initial hospitalization in Florida. An electrocardiogram (Panel A) shows sinus bradycardia, a ventricular ectopic beat, borderline first-degree atrioventricular delay, delayed intraventricular conduction, and a normal frontal-plane QRS axis. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained in a parasternal long-axis view (Panel B) shows mildly increased thickness of the interventricular septum (measuring 13 mm) and a mildly dilated left ventricle (measuring 60 mm at end diastole). Cardiac MRI was also performed. A fat-suppressed, T2-weighted image obtained in a short-axis view (Panel C) shows a hyperintense septum (arrows), a finding consistent with myocardial edema. An image with late gadolinium enhancement, obtained in a short-axis view (Panel D), shows patchy enhancement in the septum at the subepicardial location, with extension into the subendocardial layer of the midanterior segment; subepicardial gadolinium enhancement is also seen in the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle (arrows). An image with late gadolinium enhancement, obtained in a four-chamber view (Panel E), shows nodular foci in the midwall of the septum, as well as subepicardial gadolinium enhancement in the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle (arrows). Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of obstructive coronary disease. On ventriculography, the left ventricle was mildly and diffusely hypokinetic, and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure was 22 mm Hg (normal range, 8 to 15). Transthoracic echocardiography (Figure 1B) revealed a dilated left ventricle with an end-diastolic dimension of 60 mm (normal range, 42 to 58) and an ejection fraction of 35% (normal range, 55 to 70); there was diffuse hypokinesis that was most notable in the inferior and septal territories, mildly increased wall thickness, and mild mitral regurgitation (seeVideo 1, available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed the septal hypokinesis and revealed moderate left ventricular dilatation with an ejection fraction of 43%, as well as mild right ventricular dilatation with an ejection fraction of 36% (seeVideos 2 and 3, available at NEJM.org). The left ventricular myocardium was normal in thickness. T2-weighted images (Figure 1C) showed marked myocardial edema that was most prominent in the interventricular septum. The ratio of signal in the myocardium to signal in the skeletal muscle was elevated, at 2.4 (normal range, ≤1.9), a finding compatible with edema. Images with late gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1D and 1E) showed patchy, nodular foci in the midwall and subepicardium of the septum and in the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle, with minimal extension into the subendocardium of the anterior segment at the midventricular level. The myocardial edema and pattern of late gadolinium enhancement fulfilled the Lake Louise criteria for the diagnosis of acute myocarditis.1,2 Additional laboratory test results included negative nucleic acid amplification tests of the blood for DNA of adenovirus,Chlamydophila pneumoniae, cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, andMycoplasma pneumoniae, as well as negative nucleic acid amplification tests of a nasopharyngeal swab for DNA ofBordetella pertussis, coronavirus, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and rhinovirus. In addition, serologic testing was negative for antibodies to coxsackievirus, human immunodeficiency virus types 1 and 2, Lyme disease, andTrypanosoma cruzi, as well as for IgM antibodies to cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus viral capsid antigen, and parvovirus. Aspirin, metoprolol succinate, and amiodarone were prescribed, and the patient was discharged with a wearable defibrillator vest after a follow-up visit had been scheduled at this hospital. Ten days before this admission, the patient had consultations at this hospital with a cardiologist specializing in the management of heart failure and an electrophysiologist. Vital signs were notable for a heart rate of 49 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 108/70 mm Hg; the examination was otherwise normal. An electrocardiogram (Figure 2A) showed sinus bradycardia and first-degree atrioventricular delay, as well as right bundle-branch block and a left anterior fascicular block (which together constitute bifascicular block). Aspirin was stopped, spironolactone was added, and placement of an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) was scheduled. Subsequent Cardiac Studies, Obtained at This Hospital.An electrocardiogram obtained during the patient’s visit to an outpatient clinic at this hospital, 10 days before admission (Panel A), shows sinus bradycardia, first-degree atrioventricular delay, and progression to right bundle-branch block and left anterior fascicular block (which together constitute bifascicular block). A follow-up electrocardiogram obtained shortly after implantation of the implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) at this hospital (Panel B) shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with an extremely wide QRS complex. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained in a parasternal long-axis view shortly after the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit of this hospital (Panel C) shows thinning of the interventricular septum (arrow), which had decreased in thickness from 13 mm to 7 mm during the 4-week period since the initial echocardiogram had been obtained. On the morning of this admission, during placement of a dual-chamber ICD, episodes of ventricular tachycardia with varying foci were induced. These episodes were terminated with overdrive pacing. After the procedure, ventricular tachycardia developed, with a heart rate of 108 beats per minute (Figure 2B). The blood pressure was 88/53 mm Hg, and a lidocaine infusion was administered. Laboratory test results are shown inTable 1. During the next 10 hours, multiple additional episodes of monomorphic ventricular rhythms occurred, with the heart rate ranging from 90 to 140 beats per minute. The rate of lidocaine infusion was increased, and amiodarone was administered. Early in the morning of the second hospital day, ventricular tachycardia recurred, with associated dyspnea and a blood pressure of 66/40 mm Hg. Normal saline and norepinephrine were administered intravenously. Chest radiography revealed ICD leads in the appropriate position, and bedside echocardiography revealed no evidence of pericardial effusion. The ventricular tachycardia was terminated with antitachycardic pacing, and the ICD was reprogrammed to provide atrial pacing at a rate of 110 beats per minute. During this period, she has had frequent headaches, difficulty sleeping, and increased sweating. She has not had any weight changes. Over the past year, menses occurred at irregular 30- to 45-day intervals with light flow. The patient underwent two successful cesarean sections at the ages of 28 and 32. She has two healthy children. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use condoms. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Estradiol 8 pg/mL (mid-follicular phase: N=27‚Äì123 pg/mL)
Follicle-stimulating hormone 200 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 180 mIU/mL
Prolactin 16 ng/mL
What is the most likely diagnosis?"

sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.
The patient is a 36-year-old woman with amenorrhea for four months.
She's had irregular periods over the past year, with intervals of 30-45 days and light flow.
No weight changes, which might rule out something like anorexia or hyperthyroidism.
She's had two cesarean sections before, but that's probably not directly related.
She's sexually active without condoms, so pregnancy is a consideration, but the lab results might point elsewhere.
Her symptoms include headaches, trouble sleeping, and increased sweating.
Those could be due to hormonal imbalances.
The lab results are key here.
Let's look at the hormone levels.
Estradiol is low (8 pg/mL vs normal mid-follicular phase 27-123).
FSH is super high (200 mIU/mL) and LH is also elevated (180).

Prolactin is normal at 16 ng/mL. 

Wait, normally, in conditions like menopause, both FSH and LH would be high, but she's 36, which is young.
So maybe premature ovarian failure (now called primary ovarian insufficiency)?
That's when the ovaries stop working properly before age 40.
The high FSH and LH with low estradiol fit that.
But let's think of other possibilities.
Maybe a pituitary issue?
If there was a pituitary adenoma, like a prolactinoma, prolactin would be elevated, but here it's normal.
So prolactinoma is less likely.
Another thought: ovarian resistance syndrome?
That's where the ovaries don't respond to FSH, leading to high levels.
But that's usually genetic and might present with similar hormone levels.
Or maybe she's in menopause early?
Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) is the term now.
The high FSH (typically over 40 is a cutoff) definitely supports that.
Since her FSH is 200, that's way above.
Other differentials: thyroid dysfunction?
But her prolactin is normal, and thyroid issues might affect other hormones.
Also, she has no weight change.
So putting it all together: amenorrhea, high FSH/LH, low estradiol, young age.
The most likely is primary ovarian insufficiency.
The lab results are classic for that.
The headaches could be due to estrogen withdrawal or other factors, but the key is the hormone levels.
She might need further testing like AMH levels, but the labs here are pointing to POI.

prompt: A 45-year-old female presents to the outpatient clinic with symptoms of pain, fatigue and weakness in both lower limbs. She gives history of paralysis affecting both lower limbs in childhood from which she made good functional recovery.

sentences.s: Okay, let's see.
The patient is a 45-year-old woman presenting with pain, fatigue, and weakness in both lower limbs.
She has a history of childhood paralysis that she recovered from.
Hmm, so the key points here are the current symptoms of lower limb weakness and pain, along with a past history of similar issues in childhood.
First, I need to think about possible causes of lower limb weakness and pain.
The fact that she had a similar issue in childhood that she recovered from might be a clue.
Maybe it's a condition that can have relapses or progression over time.
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) comes to mind because it's a demyelinating disease that can have relapsing-remitting courses.
But MS typically affects different parts of the central nervous system, not necessarily the same area.
Also, the initial episode in childhood might not fit perfectly unless it was the first attack.
But the question mentions "paralysis affecting both lower limbs" in childhood, which might suggest a spinal cord issue.
Another thought is spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), but that's usually a genetic disorder presenting in infancy or childhood, and it's progressive.
Since she made a good recovery, maybe not SMA.
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is a possibility, but that's usually acute onset, ascending paralysis, and typically preceded by an infection.
The history here mentions a childhood episode, so maybe not GBS unless it's a recurrence, but GBS is usually a single episode.
Maybe a neuromuscular disorder like myasthenia gravis?
But myasthenia usually has fluctuating muscle weakness, often in the eyes or face, and can be treated with medications.
The current symptoms are in the lower limbs, which is less common.
Wait, the key here is the history of childhood paralysis with recovery.
That makes me think of conditions like poliomyelitis.
Polio can cause paralysis, and if she recovered, she might have post-polio syndrome later in life.
Post-polio syndrome typically presents decades after the initial infection with progressive weakness, fatigue, and muscle atrophy.
The symptoms here are pain, fatigue, and weakness in the legs, which aligns with that.
So, post-polio syndrome is a strong candidate.
Let me check the details again.
The patient is 45, so if she had polio as a child, say 30 years ago, that's within the timeframe when post-polio syndrome can occur.
The symptoms of new weakness and fatigue, especially in the same limbs affected before, fit.
Other possibilities?
Maybe a spinal cord tumor or something compressing the spine, but the history of prior paralysis and recovery makes me lean more towards a post-viral syndrome.
Alternatively, could it be a different type of muscular dystrophy that has a later onset?
But most muscular dystrophies present earlier.
So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is post-polio syndrome.
The combination of prior polio with recovery and now new symptoms decades later fits.

<answer>
Post-polio syndrome
</answer>

What causes that in the context of tobacco use?
Maybe it's not cancer.
Let's think.
Trismus can be due to several things.
Temporomandibular joint issues?
Like arthritis or injury?
But she's been using tobacco for a long time.
Another thought: fibrosis or scarring from chronic irritation.
Oh right, tobacco chewing often leads to leukoplakia or other lesions, but she doesn't have ulcers.
Wait, maybe the constant irritation from the tobacco is causing fibrosis in the muscles or the TMJ area.
Oh, there's a condition called "tobacco quid-induced trismus" or something similar.

I think that's a thing.
The chronic irritation from keeping tobacco in the mouth can lead to fibrotic changes in the buccal mucosa.

Wait, another possibility: oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF).

That's a condition associated with chewing betel nut and tobacco.

The hallmark is that the tissues become fibrotic, so the patient can't open their mouth properly.
The absence of ulcers makes sense because OSMF presents with fibrosis rather than ulcers, though sometimes there can be blisters early on that resolve into fibrosis.
So putting it all together: chronic tobacco use leading to oral submucous fibrosis, resulting in trismus.
That fits the presentation.

prompt: A 30-year-old woman presented to the emergency department of this hospital with chills and sudden worsening of abdominal pain in both lower quadrants. The patient was in her usual good health until 10 days before admission, when, after eating at a restaurant, she had nonbloody, nonbilious emesis that she attributed to food poisoning. The vomiting persisted for 2 days and then resolved. One day later, bilateral abdominal pain developed; the pain waxed and waned for a few days. She then completed a 2-day driving trip as part of her relocation to New England for a new job. During the trip, she had watery, nonbloody diarrhea every time she tried to eat (about four times per day). Her travel companion ate foods that were similar to the foods she ate but was well. After the patient arrived at her final destination, chills, fevers, and “sharp” abdominal pain in both lower quadrants, with bloating, developed. She took naproxen every 8 hours for the pain and noted some improvement. She had minimal appetite, and she noted that the frequency of the diarrheal episodes decreased when her eating decreased. However, abdominal pain persisted and intensified until she rated it as 9 to 10 on a scale of 0 to 10, with 10 indicating the most severe pain. Two nights later, she was seen in the emergency department of this hospital because of abdominal pain and distention, diarrhea, and chills. On arrival, the patient reported nausea and increased abdominal pain without further episodes of emesis. There was no hematochezia, melena, vaginal discharge, dysuria, or foul-smelling urine. Menarche had occurred at 12 years of age. Her menstrual periods occurred in normal 30-day cycles; her most recent menstrual period had been 2 weeks before this presentation. She had had no known contact with persons who were ill. She had no chest, flank, back, or neck pain, no dyspnea, and no swelling or pain in the calves. She had not lost weight. The patient had a history of a 1-cm ovarian cyst, which had been identified during her early teenage years. She was of East Asian descent, had lived in the Midwest for the previous 10 years, and worked in a medical field. At presentation, she was taking no medications except naproxen, as well as ibuprofen for pain during menstruation. She had no known drug allergies. She did not smoke or use alcohol or illicit drugs. She had never been sexually active. Her father had diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. There was no family history of cancer. On examination, the temperature was 36.5°C, the heart rate 129 beats per minute, the blood pressure 123/66 mm Hg, the respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 97% while the patient was breathing ambient air. Her body was well developed. She appeared to be uncomfortable except when she was lying flat. She appeared to be flushed, but there was no scleral icterus or rash. She had tachycardia, but the cardiac examination was otherwise normal. The abdomen was mildly distended, with tenderness in both lower quadrants that was worst in the midline; there was voluntary guarding on palpation but no rebound, and bowel sounds were diminished. The remainder of the examination was normal. Results of coagulation tests were normal, as were red-cell indexes and blood levels of magnesium and globulin; other test results are shown inTable 1. Two sets of blood culture specimens and a urine culture specimen were obtained. A chest radiograph showed low lung volumes and patchy bibasilar opacities. A urine test for human chorionic gonadotropin was negative. Laboratory Data. Intravenous normal saline, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and morphine were administered. Imaging studies were obtained and additional diagnostic procedures were performed.
true_dx: Acutely inflamed endometriotic cyst with overlying acute peritonitis involving the ovarian surface as well as the fallopian tube and appendix.

prompt: A 7-year old patient p. its with headache, paralysis of upward gaze, loss of ilOtt perception and accommodation, nystagmus and failure of convergence. CT scan showed homogenous hyperdense lesion above the sella and in the posterior pa of the third ventricle. MRI showed that the lesions were homogenous and isointense on T1 weighted imaging, and isointense onT2 weighted imaging with intense contrast enhancement.

sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.
The patient is a 7-year-old with some neurological symptoms.

The main symptoms mentioned are headache, paralysis of upward gaze, loss of pupillary light reflex (since "ilOtt" might be a typo for "pupillary" or "light reflex"), accommodation issues, nystagmus, and failure of convergence.
First, I need to think about the neurological signs.
Paralysis of upward gaze and issues with eye movements like nystagmus and convergence failure point towards a problem affecting the cranial nerves involved in eye movement.
The third cranial nerve (oculomotor) is responsible for most eye movements, including upward gaze.
However, the loss of pupillary light reflex (if that's what "ilOtt" refers to) is also a sign of oculomotor nerve involvement because the third nerve controls the parasympathetic input to the pupil.
But the imaging findings are key here.
The CT shows a homogeneous hyperdense lesion above the sella turcica and in the posterior part of the third ventricle.
Hyperdensity on CT usually suggests hemorrhage, calcification, or a mass with high density like a meningioma.
However, the MRI findings are important too.
On T1 and T2, the lesion is isointense but enhances intensely with contrast.
That enhancement suggests a vascular structure or a tumor with active growth, like a meningioma or a craniopharyngioma.
Wait, craniopharyngioma is a common pediatric brain tumor.
It typically occurs near the sellar region, so above the sella makes sense.
They are often cystic but can have calcifications, leading to hyperdensity on CT.
The MRI characteristics of isointense signals on both T1 and T2 with strong enhancement fit craniopharyngioma.
The location near the pituitary area could explain the endocrine issues, but the main symptoms here are related to the eye movements.
The third ventricle involvement might compress the nearby structures, like the optic chiasm or the oculomotor nerves.
The upward gaze palsy could be due to compression of the oculomotor nerves (CN III) as they exit the midbrain.
The loss of accommodation and pupillary light reflex (if that's the case) also points to CN III issues.
Another possibility is a Rathke's cleft cyst, but those usually don't enhance as much.
A meningioma could also be in that location, but they are less common in children.
The intense enhancement and the location in the posterior third ventricle make me think of craniopharyngioma.
The symptoms align with the anatomical location compressing the surrounding structures, leading to those eye movement abnormalities.

So putting it all together: the imaging findings (hyperdense on CT, isointense on MRI with strong enhancement) and the clinical presentation (eye movement issues due to CN III compression) point to a craniopharyngioma.

<answer>
Craniopharyngioma
</answer>

prompt: A 6-year-old boy is taken to a paediatrician because he has developed pain in his right hip. On physical examination, the doctor feels a large mass near the iliac crest. Plain X-ray films demonstrate a large lytic lesion of the ilium. MRI studies show that the tumor appears to arise in the bone, but extends into the adjacent soft tissues. A large incisional biopsy demonstrates a tumor composed of sheets of small, round, blue cells.

sentences.s: Okay, let's see.
The case is a 6-year-old boy with hip pain and a mass near the iliac crest.
The X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the ilium.
MRI shows the tumor starts in the bone and extends into soft tissues.
The biopsy shows sheets of small, round, blue cells.
Hmm.
First, the age is important.
A 6-year-old is a child, so I should think of pediatric bone tumors.
The most common primary bone tumors in kids are osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma.
Osteosarcoma usually occurs in adolescents, around the time of growth spurts, often in the metaphysis of long bones like the femur or tibia.
But this is the ilium, which is a flat bone.
Ewing sarcoma can occur in various bones, including the pelvis, and is more common in kids.
The X-ray shows a lytic lesion.
Both osteosarcoma and Ewing can be lytic, but Ewing is more purely lytic, while osteosarcoma might have more mineralization or a sunburst appearance on X-ray.
The MRI shows extension into soft tissues, which both can do, but the key here is the biopsy result.
The biopsy shows small, round, blue cells.
That's a classic description for small round blue cell tumors.
The differential for that includes Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (EWS/PNET), neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, etc.
But in bone, the main ones are Ewing and osteosarcoma.
Osteosarcoma cells are more spindle or osteoblastic, not small round blue cells.
So that points more towards Ewing.
Also, Ewing sarcoma typically arises in bone but can invade soft tissues.
The location in the pelvis is common for Ewing.
Osteosarcoma of the pelvis does occur but is less common, and the histology wouldn't match.
Another thought: Could it be a metastatic tumor?
But in a 6-year-old, primary tumors are more likely.
Neuroblastoma usually starts in the adrenal gland, but could metastasize to bone.
However, the primary would likely be elsewhere.
The biopsy is from the bone lesion, so if it's small round cells in bone, Ewing is still top.
Also, Ewing sarcoma is associated with the t(11;22) translocation, which leads to expression of a fusion protein.
But without molecular testing, the histology and clinical presentation are key here.
The combination of age, bone location (pelvis), lytic lesion, and small round blue cells on biopsy all point to Ewing sarcoma.

Another angle: the well-demarcated rash in the groin of an athlete.
Tinea is super common in this scenario.
The spared scrotum is a bit confusing, but maybe the infection is on the thighs and perineum, which are areas where the fungus can thrive in warm, moist environments from sweating during sports.
Contact dermatitis is also possible, but the classic "jock itch" is more likely given the presentation and risk factors.
Wait, but contact dermatitis can be from the mats, sweat, or even soap.
The well-demarcated borders can occur if the irritant was in a specific area.
However, the most common diagnosis in a wrestler with groin rash is tinea cruris.
The fact that the scrotum is spared might be because the infection is on the non-hairy areas, and the scrotum's skin is different.
Alternatively, maybe the rash is on the thighs and perineum, which are areas where the fungus can grow, while the scrotum's skin is less hospitable.
So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is tinea cruris, commonly known as jock itch.
The key points are the athlete's activity, the location, the pruritus, and the well-demarcated erythema.

prompt: A 39-year-old man repos seeing red-colored urine in the morning. The CBC reveals anemia, low serum iron, and an elevated reticulocyte count. Laboratory studies show increased lysis of erythrocytes when incubated with either sucrose or acidified serum.

sentences.s: Okay, let's tackle this case.
The patient is a 39-year-old man with red-colored urine in the morning.
The first thing that comes to mind is hematuria, but the red color could also be due to hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria.
The CBC shows anemia and low serum iron, which suggests that there's blood loss or increased red cell destruction.
The elevated reticulocyte count indicates that the bone marrow is trying to compensate by producing more red blood cells, so this is likely a hemolytic anemia.
Now, the key lab findings here are increased lysis of erythrocytes when incubated with sucrose or acidified serum.
I remember that in certain hemolytic disorders, the red blood cells are more susceptible to breakdown under specific conditions.
Let me think...
The sucrose test is part of the osmotic fragility test.
